name: Words trivia (easy)
description: 50 easy questions about word meanings, origins, spelling, idioms, grammar. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: The English word 'salary' comes from the Latin 'salarium', which is linked to the Latin word for what?
items.explain: 'Salary' derives from Latin 'salarium', which is linked to 'sal', the Latin word for salt. Whether Roman soldiers were actually paid in salt is disputed.

source.title: Our pay is called a 'salary,' but were Roman soldiers really paid in salt?

items.question: In the theatre, what do you wish a performer when you tell them to 'break a leg'?
items.explain: 'Break a leg' is an idiom meaning good luck, said to a performer before going on stage.

source.title: Break A Leg - Meaning & Origin Of The Phrase

items.question: What does the idiom 'it's raining cats and dogs' mean?
answers: It is about to stop raining
It is raining during a storm
items.explain: The idiom describes extremely heavy rain. It has nothing to do with real animals falling from the sky.

source.title: It's Raining Cats and Dogs

items.question: If a task is described as 'a piece of cake', what does that mean?
items.explain: 'A piece of cake' is an idiom for something that is very easy to do.

source.title: Crack the Code of American Idioms: A Guide for Immigrants

items.question: What does it mean to 'spill the beans'?
items.explain: The idiom has nothing to do with real beans. It means to reveal secret information.

source.title: Crack the Code of American Idioms: A Guide for Immigrants

items.question: What does the idiom 'bite the bullet' mean?
answers: Give up on a goal early
items.explain: To 'bite the bullet' is to decide to do something difficult or unpleasant that you have been putting off.

source.title: Crack the Code of American Idioms: A Guide for Immigrants

items.question: What is an idiom?
answers: A word that imitates a sound
A phrase that reads the same backward
A word that sounds like another word
A phrase whose meaning isn't clear from its words
items.correct: A phrase whose meaning isn't clear from its words
items.explain: An idiom is a commonly known phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from the ordinary meanings of its individual words.

source.title: Crack the Code of American Idioms: A Guide for Immigrants

items.question: What does the idiom 'break the ice' mean?
items.explain: 'Break the ice' means to get a conversation going in an awkward or unfamiliar situation.

source.title: American English Idioms: Expressions Only Americans Use

items.question: If someone 'hits the nail on the head', what have they done?
items.explain: 'Hit the nail on the head' means to be exactly right about something.

source.title: American English Idioms: Expressions Only Americans Use

items.question: If you say you are 'under the weather', how are you feeling?
items.explain: 'Under the weather' is an idiom meaning feeling sick or unwell.

source.title: American English Idioms: Expressions Only Americans Use

items.question: If something 'costs an arm and a leg', what is true of it?
items.explain: 'Cost an arm and a leg' is an idiom meaning something is very expensive.

source.title: American English Idioms: Expressions Only Americans Use

items.question: The sandwich is said to be named after which English nobleman?
items.explain: The story goes that John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich, was too busy to stop for dinner and asked for beef between slices of bread.

source.title: Are 'sandwich' and 'cardigan' named after real people? - CSMonitor.com

items.question: The word 'boycott' comes from the name of a land agent who was shunned by tenants in which country?
items.explain: The term comes from Captain Charles C. Boycott, a land agent who was ostracized by the Irish.

source.title: What Is an Eponym? Meaning and Popular Examples

items.question: The word 'pasteurize' is named after which French scientist?
items.explain: 'Pasteurize' comes from Louis Pasteur, honored for his work in food safety.

source.title: 50 Words Named After People: The Fascinating World of Eponyms

items.question: The name 'America' honors which Italian mapmaker?
items.explain: America is named after the Italian mapmaker Amerigo Vespucci.

source.title: What Is an Eponym? Meaning, Definition and 10 Examples

items.question: The saxophone is named after which Belgian instrument maker?
items.explain: The saxophone takes its name from Adolphe Sax, the Belgian instrument maker who invented it.

source.title: 50 Words Named After People: The Fascinating World of Eponyms

items.question: The word 'sideburns' comes from the surname of which American general?
items.explain: 'Sideburns' is an eponym from Ambrose Burnside, known for his distinctive facial hair.

source.title: What Is an Eponym? Meaning and Popular Examples

items.question: Who is the Caesar salad named after?
items.explain: The salad was created by restaurateur Caesar Cardini and bears his name. It has nothing to do with the Roman rulers.

source.title: What Is an Eponym? Meaning, Definition and 10 Examples

items.question: The cardigan sweater is named after an earl who led which 1854 military action?
answers: The Charge of the Light Brigade
items.correct: The Charge of the Light Brigade
items.explain: The garment is named after James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan, who led the Charge of the Light Brigade during the Crimean War.

source.title: Are 'sandwich' and 'cardigan' named after real people? - CSMonitor.com

items.question: The women's garment called 'bloomers' is named after which women's rights activist?
items.explain: Bloomers take their name from the women's rights activist Amelia Bloomer.

source.title: What Is an Eponym? Meaning and Popular Examples

items.question: What is a word that is named after a person, such as 'diesel', called?
items.explain: An eponym is a word named after a person or place. 'Diesel' comes from Rudolf Diesel.

source.title: What Is an Eponym? Meaning, Definition and 10 Examples

items.question: Which language did English borrow the word 'algebra' from?
items.explain: 'Algebra' comes from the Arabic 'al-jabr', meaning a reunion of broken parts.

source.title: English Words Borrowed From Arabic

items.question: In English words like 'alcohol' and 'algebra', the opening 'al-' comes from an Arabic word meaning what?
items.explain: The 'al-' at the start of these loanwords is the Arabic definite article, meaning 'the'.

source.title: Arabic words in English - How They Came to Be

items.question: Which drink's English name traces back, via Turkish and Dutch, to the Arabic word 'qahwa'?
items.explain: 'Coffee' entered English via Dutch 'koffie', from Ottoman Turkish 'kahve', which came from Arabic 'qahwa'.

source.title: Arabic coffee

items.question: The contraction 'they're' is short for which two words?
items.explain: The apostrophe in 'they're' shows it is two words joined: 'they' and 'are'.

source.title: "Their" vs. "There" vs. "They're": What's the Difference?

items.question: Which word correctly completes this sentence: 'The kids forgot ___ umbrellas at school'?
items.explain: 'Their' is the possessive form of 'they', meaning belonging to them.

source.title: "There" vs. "Their" vs. "They're": What's the Difference?

items.question: Which word correctly completes this sentence: '___ welcome to join us for dinner'?
items.explain: 'You're' is a contraction of 'you are', and the sentence needs 'you are'.

source.title: Homophones and Contractions : Grammar & Editing Tips

items.question: What are words that sound alike but differ in meaning, such as 'their' and 'there', called?
items.explain: Homophones are words with the same pronunciation but different meanings, and often different spellings.

source.title: Their vs There vs They're

items.question: What does the Latin abbreviation 'e.g.' mean?
items.explain: 'E.g.' stands for the Latin 'exempli gratia', which means 'for example'.

source.title: Latin Terms and Abbreviations

items.question: What does the Latin abbreviation 'i.e.' mean?
items.explain: 'I.e.' is from the Latin 'id est', meaning 'that is'. It is used to clarify what was just said.

source.title: E.g. and I.e.: Choosing the Right Abbreviation

items.question: What figure of speech compares two things using the words 'like' or 'as'?
items.explain: A simile says one thing is 'like' or 'as' another. A metaphor says one thing simply is another.

source.title: Similes and Metaphors

items.question: Which of these words is a palindrome, reading the same backward as forward?
items.explain: 'Racecar' is spelled the same in both directions, which makes it a palindrome.

source.title: Palindromes Defined: 9 Types of Palindromes

items.question: The famous palindrome 'A man, a plan, a canal' ends with the name of which country?
items.explain: The palindrome 'A man, a plan, a canal, Panama' refers to the building of the Panama Canal.

source.title: Palindrome

items.question: What is it called when you rearrange the letters of a word or phrase to spell a different one?
items.explain: Rearranging a word's letters to make another word or phrase is an anagram. A palindrome reads the same backward.

source.title: What Is the Longest Palindrome in English?

items.question: A word that imitates the sound it describes, like 'buzz' or 'clang', is an example of what?
items.explain: Onomatopoeia is a figure of speech in which a word imitates the sound associated with an action or object.

source.title: Onomatopoeia

items.question: Words like 'wow' and 'ugh', which express emotion rather than a specific sound, are usually classed as what?
items.explain: Outbursts that express emotion rather than a specific sound are interjections or exclamations, not onomatopoeia.

source.title: 50 Onomatopoeia Examples That You Never Thought of Before

items.question: Which of these phrases is a classic example of an oxymoron?
items.explain: An oxymoron pairs words that seem to have opposite meanings, and 'jumbo' (big) with 'shrimp' (small) is a standard example.

source.title: OXYMORON

items.question: Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis, the longest word in major dictionaries, names a disease of which body part?
items.explain: It is defined as a lung disease caused by inhaling very fine silicate or quartz dust.

source.title: The Longest Word in the Dictionary

items.question: Complete the spelling rhyme: 'I before E, except after ...'
items.explain: The rhyme says 'i before e, except after c', which covers words like 'receive' and 'ceiling'.

source.title: I Before E Except After C: Is it a rule?

items.question: Which of these words breaks the 'i before e' spelling rule?
items.explain: 'Weird' has 'ei' even though there is no 'c' before it. Seize and height are other well-known exceptions.

source.title: I Before E Except After C: Is it a rule?

items.question: Which of these is the correct spelling?
items.explain: The middle vowel is 'a', not 'e'. A common memory trick is that there is 'a rat' in sepARATe.

source.title: Commonly Misspelled Words

items.question: Which of these is the correct spelling?
items.explain: The word contains 'finite', so there is no 'a' in it.

source.title: Commonly Misspelled Words

items.question: Which of these is the correct spelling?
items.explain: The word has a double 'c' and a double 'm'.

source.title: Commonly Misspelled Words

items.question: Which of these is the correct spelling?
items.explain: The word has a double 'r' and a double 's'. It is one of the most commonly misspelled English words.

source.title: Commonly Misspelled Words

items.question: Which of these is the correct spelling?
items.explain: The correct spelling has one 'c' and a double 's'.

source.title: 100 Commonly Misspelled Words in English [With Tricks]

items.question: Which of these is the correct spelling of a day of the week?
items.explain: It is spelled with a silent 'd' and the 'ne' in the middle: Wed-nes-day.

source.title: 100 Commonly Misspelled Words in English [With Tricks]

items.question: Which of these is the correct spelling of a month?
items.explain: The first 'r' is often dropped in speech but belongs in the spelling: Feb-ru-ary.

source.title: 100 Commonly Misspelled Words in English [With Tricks]

items.question: Which of these is the correct spelling?
items.explain: The word is spelled with 'rh' at the start and 'th' in the middle.

source.title: 100 Commonly Misspelled Words in English [With Tricks]

items.question: Which of these is the correct spelling?
items.explain: 'Concensus' is a common misspelling. The correct word is 'consensus', which is built on 'consent', not 'census'.

source.title: Commonly misspelled English words

items.question: Which of these is the correct spelling?
items.explain: The word has 'au' in the middle: rest-au-rant.

source.title: 100 Commonly Misspelled Words in English [With Tricks]
